questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Is Asked
This tests practical policy design, edge-case handling, and CI integration for Kubernetes manifests in a multi-team environment. Candidates must demonstrate understanding of resource isolation, pod hardening, network security, and hardware scheduling constraints.

## Key Concepts
- **ResourceQuota and LimitRange**: Prevent resource starvation and enforce default resource requests/limits per namespace
- **Pod securityContext**: Enforce runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capability dropping for workload hardening
- **Ingress TLS with cert-manager**: Ensure encrypted external traffic with automated certificate management
- **GPU scheduling constraints**: Use nodeSelector and resource requests to restrict GPU workloads to approved namespaces and nodes
- **CI validation**: Integrate Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper with kubectl dry-run for pre-merge enforcement

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno ClusterPolicy for ML Platform Gates
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-ml-platform-gates
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
    - name: require-resource-quota
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Namespace]
      validate:
        message: "Each namespace must have a ResourceQuota."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              quota-ready: "true"

    - name: require-security-context
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
      validate:
        message: "Containers must run as non-root with read-only filesystem and drop ALL capabilities."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - securityContext:
                  runAsNonRoot: true
                  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
                  capabilities:
                    drop: [ALL]

    - name: require-ingress-tls
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Ingress]
      validate:
        message: "Ingress must use TLS with cert-manager annotation."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            annotations:
              (cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer): "?*"
          spec:
            tls:
              - secretName: "?*"

    - name: gpu-in-approved-namespaces
      match:
        resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
      preconditions:
        - key: "nvidia.com/gpu"
          operator: In
          value: ["1", "2", "4"]
      validate:
        message: "GPU pods are only allowed in approved namespaces with nvidia nodeSelector."
        pattern:
          spec:
            nodeSelector:
              nvidia.com/gpu: "?*"
```

## Verification Strategy

**Local Testing:**
```bash
# Install Kyverno
kubectl apply -f policy.yaml

# Dry-run validate manifests
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f manifest.yaml

# Test policy against sample manifests
kyverno apply policy.yaml --manifest manifest.yaml
```

**CI Integration (GitHub Actions):**
```yaml
name: Manifest Validation
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Validate with Kyverno
        run: |
          kyverno apply cluster-policy.yaml \
            --manifest manifests/ \
            --policy-report \
            --fail-only-on-exists
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical policy-as-code skills and integration of admission controls into CI for a multi-cloud, large-scale platform.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper/OPA ConstraintTemplate
- securityContext runAsNonRoot and runAsUser
- privileged and capabilities.drop
- hostPath/hostIPC/hostPID prohibition
- CI validation with kubectl/dry-run and Gatekeeper

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (high-level sketch)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sprivilege
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sPrivilege
  targets:
  - target: AdmissionReview
    rego: |
      package k8sprivilege
      violation["privilege violation"] {
        input.review.object.kind == "Deployment"
      }
```
```yaml
# Failing manifest (hostPath & privileged)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: bad-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: example/app:latest
          securityContext:
            privileged: true
            runAsNonRoot: false
            runAsUser: 0
            capabilities:
              drop: []
      volumes:
        - name: data
          hostPath:
            path: /tmp
            type: Directory
```
```yaml
# Passing manifest (non-root, restricted caps, no hostPath)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: good-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: example/app:latest
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            privileged: false
            capabilities:
              drop:
                - ALL
      volumes: []
```

- Run Gatekeeper in CI and verify failing/passing manifests via kubectl apply --dry-run and gatekeeper playbooks.
- Confirm PRs fail on bad manifests and pass on good manifests.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests foundational secure supply chain practices in a beginner-friendly manner. It mirrors real-world CI gates used in production environments around Dockerfile hygiene, image signing, SBOM generation, and registry controls. It introduces modern tools like Cosign and SBOM attestations without overwhelming complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Dockerfile Hygiene**: Non-root USER and multi-stage builds reduce security vulnerabilities and image size
- **Container Image Signing**: Using Cosign to sign and verify container images ensures integrity
- **SBOM Attestation**: Software Bill of Materials provides transparency into image contents and dependencies
- **GitHub Actions Workflows**: Implementing gates and policy checks in CI/CD pipelines
- **Registry Allowlist**: Restricting deployments to approved registries prevents supply chain attacks

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Docker Security Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Validate Dockerfile
        run: |
          # Check for non-root USER
          grep -q 'USER ' Dockerfile || exit 1
          # Check for multi-stage build
          grep -q 'FROM.*AS' Dockerfile || exit 1
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json > sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign image and SBOM with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --type spdx-json --predicate sbom.json ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Verify signature and attestation
        run: |
          cosign verify ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
```

# ConstraintTemplate for Gatekeeper enforcing egress gateway annotation
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1

## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates hands-on policy-as-code skills using Gatekeeper/OPA, Kubernetes security contexts, and CI validation in realistic multi-tenant sandbox environments. It assesses understanding of admission control, namespace isolation, and resource governance.

## Key Concepts

- **ConstraintTemplate vs. Constraint**: A ConstraintTemplate defines the Rego policy logic and CRD schema; a Constraint is a specific instance that applies the policy to matching resources.
- **Kubernetes resource requests/limits**: Requests define minimum guaranteed resources; limits define the maximum resources a container can consume.
- **Security contexts**: These define pod-level and container-level security settings, including running as non-root and read-only filesystems.
- **Namespace isolation**: Gatekeeper policies can target specific namespaces using the `startswith` function to match patterns like `sandbox-*`.
- **Comprehensive validation**: The policy must validate ALL containers in a Deployment, not just check if ANY container meets requirements.

## Evaluation Criteria

A strong answer demonstrates:
1. Correct Rego logic that validates every container (not just the first match)
2. Proper separation between ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
3. Working test cases that actually exercise each validation rule
4. Understanding of the baseline resource concept (50-200% range)
5. CI/CD integration steps for automated validation

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a scalable, automated policy gate across multi-cloud clusters using Gatekeeper/OPA, Cosign attestations, and runtime security constraints.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- Cosign attestation and image provenance
- Registry allowlist and image provenance checks
- Pod security: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop capabilities
- CI integration and gatekeeper audit verification

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (Gatekeeper) minimal sketch
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8ssecuredcontainers
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sSecuredContainers
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package k8ssecuredcontainers
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not signed(container.image)
          msg := sprintf("Container image %v must be cosign-signed", [container.image])
        }
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not allowed_registry(container.image)
          msg := sprintf("Registry %v not in allowlist", [container.image])
        }
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
          msg := "Container must run as non-root"
        }
```

## What to Look For

- Demonstrates understanding of OPA/Gatekeeper policy structure
- Shows proper cosign attestation validation approach
- Includes comprehensive runtime security constraints
- Outlines practical CI/CD integration strategy
